reason: The sources fully support a myth-busting story with 15 verified two-site claims explaining the physics and engineering behind the Moon flag.
story: Conspiracy theorists often claim the Apollo 11 Moon landing was faked because the American flag appears to wave in the wind on an airless world. The reality is simple engineering and vacuum physics. Because the Moon has no atmosphere, NASA engineers knew a standard flag would hang limply against its pole. Technical services chief Jack Kinzler designed the Lunar Flag Assembly with a telescoping horizontal aluminum rod along the top hem to keep the nylon fabric extended. When Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin planted the staff, their twisting and jostling sent vibrations into the cloth. On Earth, air drag quickly stops a fluttering flag, but in the vacuum of space, with no atmospheric friction to dampen the motion, the fabric continued to swing and oscillate like a pendulum. Furthermore, permanent creases from storage gave it a rippled appearance. Once left alone, the flag stood completely still.
angle: The Apollo flag only looked like it was flapping because the vacuum of space has zero air resistance, allowing cloth to keep swinging for seconds after an astronaut touched it.

claims.claim: Six American flags were planted on the lunar surface during the Apollo program.
The Moon lacks an atmosphere, meaning there is no wind to make a flag wave.
To prevent the flag from hanging limply, NASA added a horizontal rod along the top edge to hold the fabric outstretched.
Jack Kinzler, head of technical services at the Manned Spacecraft Center, designed the flag deployment mechanism.
The flag assembly horizontal and vertical poles were constructed of gold-anodized aluminum tubes.
The flags flown on early landing missions were standard three-by-five-foot flags ordered from a government supply catalog.
The complete Lunar Flag Assembly package weighed approximately nine pounds and seven ounces.
The flag was packed inside a protective thermal shroud mounted on the Lunar Module leg or ladder to survive descent engine exhaust heat.
Movement seen in Apollo footage was caused by astronauts physically twisting, planting, and adjusting the flagpole.
In the lunar vacuum, the absence of atmospheric drag allowed the disturbed fabric to oscillate and swing longer than it would on Earth.
In video footage where no astronaut is touching or handling the flagpole, the flag remains completely motionless.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibited nations from making territorial sovereignty claims on the Moon.
Buzz Aldrin reported that the Apollo 11 flag was blown over by engine exhaust when the Lunar Module lifted off.
Orbiter imagery captured by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter showed that flags planted on later Apollo missions were still standing decades later.
NASA established the Committee on Symbolic Activities for the First Lunar Landing in early 1969 to decide on commemorative items.

disputed: Only one source asserts that the Apollo 11 horizontal crossbar jammed partially retracted to create bunched ripples, whereas other sources omit this or only cite latch issues on Apollo 12; a script should attribute this as 'according to one account' or focus on storage creases and vacuum inertia.

The exact fabric composition differs across sources, with most specifying nylon while another cites a scientist identifying rayon or modal; a script should simply describe it as standard off-the-shelf catalog fabric.
The commercial manufacturer is widely reported as Annin but NASA contractor documentation noted labels were removed; a script should avoid presenting a definitive company name as undisputed fact.

The number of surviving flags is disputed between sources confirming three upright flags (Apollo 12, 16, and 17) versus sources estimating at least five; a script should state that multiple flags from later missions remain standing.
